fields.body_text: From Forgiveness to Union Among Watchman Nee's many teachings, none has traveled more widely than the message later published in English as The Normal Christian Life. The book was assembled from addresses rather than written by Nee as a single continuous manuscript, but the theology it communicates lies close to the center of his mature ministry. It asks a question many sincere Christians eventually face: if Christ has forgiven my sins, why do I still experience such weakness, defeat, and self-effort? Nee's answer begins by distinguishing between sins and the sinner, between what we have done and what we are in Adam. The blood of Christ deals with guilt; the cross of Christ also deals with the old man. The distinction is not meant to divide the work of Christ into separate salvations but to help believers see the breadth of God's remedy. Paul writes, “God commendeth his own love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8, ASV). The gospel begins with substitution. Jesus died for us. Our sins are not excused; they are judged in the death of Another. The believer is justified by grace through faith. But Paul moves beyond forgiveness. “Our old man was crucified with him” (Romans 6:6, ASV). The preposition changes the perspective. Christ not only died for us; in a mysterious but real union, believers are said to have died with Him. For Nee, this was the doorway into sanctification. God does not merely forgive the old Adamic life and then command it to imitate Jesus more successfully. He places the believer in Christ. What happened to Christ becomes decisive for those who belong to Him. The key is union. “If we have become united with him in the likeness of his death, we shall be also in the likeness of his resurrection” (Romans 6:5, ASV). Christianity is therefore not merely moral imitation at a distance. It is participation in the life of the risen Christ. The Blood and the Cross Nee frequently contrasted the blood with the cross as a teaching device. The blood answers the problem of guilt before God. The cross answers the problem of the old self as the source of sinful living. Scripture certainly gives the blood of Christ a central place. “The blood of Jesus his Son cleanseth us from all sin” (1 John 1:7, ASV). “Being now justified by his blood, shall we be saved from the wrath of God through him” (Romans 5:9, ASV). The believer's peace with God is not based on an improved spiritual performance but on Christ's finished sacrifice. This was pastorally important to Nee. Christians who look constantly at themselves for assurance will never find a stable foundation. The blood is presented to God. Faith rests in the value God assigns to the sacrifice of His Son. The cross then addresses the deeper question of the self. Human beings do not merely commit isolated sins; they belong by nature to Adam's fallen humanity. Paul says, “as through the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, even so through the obedience of the one shall the many be made righteous” (Romans 5:19, ASV). Nee wanted believers to stop asking God merely to improve Adam. God's answer is a transfer of realm: from Adam to Christ, from death to life, from flesh to Spirit. This framework can be expressed too sharply if it implies that Scripture itself limits “blood” to forgiveness and “cross” to the self. Biblical language overlaps more than a neat theological chart suggests. Yet Nee's pastoral insight remains valuable. The gospel deals with both guilt and bondage. Christ is not only the One who cancels our debt; He is the One in whom a new humanity begins. Know Nee organized Romans 6 around several key words. The first is know. “Knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him” (Romans 6:6, ASV). Paul does not begin with a command to feel dead to sin. He begins with a fact to know. Nee emphasized this relentlessly. Christian experience must rest on God's accomplishment, not on the believer's changing emotional state. Suppose a believer wakes after a day of spiritual victory and feels close to God. He may easily believe that he is “in Christ.” The next morning he fails, becomes angry, falls into temptation, or feels spiritually cold. If his union with Christ depends on experience, his theology rises and falls with his mood. Paul places the order differently. God acted in Christ. The believer is called to know what God has done. This does not mean intellectual awareness alone creates sanctification. A person may memorize Romans 6 without living in freedom. Nee used the language of revelation to describe the moment when biblical truth becomes spiritually seen. His terminology can sound mystical, but his central point is straightforward: there is a difference between repeating a doctrine and being inwardly persuaded by it. Paul prays that the eyes of believers' hearts may be enlightened (Ephesians 1:18). Spiritual understanding is still understanding of revealed truth; it is not secret knowledge beyond Scripture. The Holy Spirit enables believers to grasp, receive, and live in what God has already made known. The word know therefore protects sanctification from becoming a self-improvement program. We begin with Christ's history, not ours. Reckon The second key word is reckon. “Even so reckon ye also yourselves to be dead unto sin, but alive unto God in Christ Jesus” (Romans 6:11, ASV). Reckoning is faith's response to fact. It does not create the fact. Nee liked illustrations from accounting: if money has truly been deposited into an account, the account holder may reckon it as present. Reckoning without a deposit would be fantasy. But refusing to reckon what has genuinely been given is unbelief. This distinction is essential. Some Christians hear “reckon yourself dead” and try to persuade themselves that temptation no longer exists. When temptation returns, they conclude that the doctrine failed. Paul is not asking believers to deny experience. He is asking them to define themselves by union with Christ rather than by the mastery of sin. Sin remains present, but it is no longer rightful lord. “Sin shall not have dominion over you: for ye are not under law, but under grace” (Romans 6:14, ASV). Reckoning is therefore not psychological make-believe. It is agreeing with God about our new position in Christ. Nee's emphasis was especially powerful for Christians trapped in repeated cycles of resolution and failure. They promise to try harder, fail, confess, rededicate, and begin again. Each cycle quietly assumes that sufficient determination will eventually produce holiness. Romans 6 announces a different starting point. The believer is not asked to strengthen the old master-servant relationship with sin but to recognize that in Christ a decisive breach has occurred. Faith says: I belong to Christ. Sin may solicit me, but it does not own me. My feelings may accuse me, but they do not define my standing. The resurrection life of Jesus is now the source from which I am called to live. Present The third movement is present. “Neither present your members unto sin as instruments of unrighteousness; but present yourselves unto God, as alive from the dead” (Romans 6:13, ASV). Knowing and reckoning lead to consecration. Grace is not passivity. The believer actively presents the body, mind, time, money, relationships, ambitions, abilities, and future to God. Notice again the order: “as alive from the dead.” We do not present ourselves in order to become alive. We present ourselves because in Christ we are alive. Nee found this sequence liberating. Consecration is not bargaining with God—“If I give You enough, perhaps You will bless me.” It is the reasonable response of a redeemed person. Romans 12 uses similar language: “present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God” (Romans 12:1, ASV). The body that once served self is now placed at God's disposal. This has practical consequences. A surrendered tongue cannot be casually given to gossip. A surrendered sexuality cannot be treated as private property. A surrendered bank account cannot be governed solely by appetite. A surrendered career cannot be exempt from obedience. A surrendered ministry cannot be owned by the minister. Nee sometimes spoke in absolute terms because he believed partial surrender is internally contradictory. If Christ is Lord, then there is no room that belongs inherently to us. Such teaching must remain rooted in grace. Consecration is not a heroic offering by which we impress God. We present what has already been purchased. Paul writes, “Ye are not your own; for ye were bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:19-20, ASV). The logic is ownership by redemption. The Failure of the Will Many believers attempt holiness primarily through willpower. Nee did not deny the importance of the will; Scripture commands choices. His objection was to treating the will as the source of spiritual life. Romans 7 dramatizes the frustration of sincere desire without adequate power: “For the good which I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I practise” (Romans 7:19, ASV). The speaker is not morally indifferent. He wants good. Yet wanting does not free him. Nee saw in Romans 7 a believer discovering the bankruptcy of self-reliance. The law is holy, but the law cannot impart power. It can reveal what righteousness looks like while exposing the inability of the flesh to produce it. The cry comes: “Wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me out of the body of this death?” (Romans 7:24, ASV). Nee loved the grammar of the question. The Law of the Spirit of Life Romans 8 introduces what Nee regarded as a new governing power. “For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus made me free from the law of sin and of death” (Romans 8:2, ASV). In the moral realm, the law of sin seems similarly persistent: left to ourselves, fallen impulses pull downward. But in Christ another law operates—the Spirit of life. Paul continues: “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God” (Romans 8:14, ASV). The Christian life is therefore not merely living by principles learned from Jesus. The believer asks God for patience and tries to become patient. Nee redirects the question: Christ Himself is our patience. The Objective and the Subjective One of Nee's useful distinctions is between the objective work of Christ and the subjective work of the Holy Spirit. Faith does not deny feelings. It refuses to enthrone them. Temptation and the Presence of Sin Some readers of victory teaching have assumed that a mature Christian should reach a state in which temptation largely disappears. fields.title: Sit: Our Position in Christ

The Strange Beginning of the Christian Life

Watchman Nee's short book Sit, Walk, Stand distilled the message of Ephesians into three verbs. Its simplicity made it memorable. The first word is the most surprising: sit. Human religion begins with activity. We ask what we must do, where we must go, what discipline we must master, what sacrifice we must make. Paul begins Ephesians somewhere else—with what God has done in Christ and where God has placed those who belong to Him.

“God, being rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us, even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ ... and raised us up with him, and made us to sit with him in the heavenly places, in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 2:4-6, ASV).

Nee saw in “sit” an entire theology of grace. A seated person is not striving to arrive at a position; he occupies one already provided. The Christian life begins not with achievement but with reception.

This is not laziness. It is order. Before the believer can walk worthily in Ephesians 4 or stand against evil in Ephesians 6, he must understand the grace announced in Ephesians 1-3. Duty grows out of identity. Practice grows out of position. The imperative is rooted in the indicative.

The principle is visible throughout Paul's letters. “If then ye were raised together with Christ, seek the things that are above” (Colossians 3:1, ASV). First, raised with Christ; then, seek. “If we live by the Spirit, by the Spirit let us also walk” (Galatians 5:25, ASV). First life; then walk.

Nee feared that many Christians reverse this order. They try to walk in order to earn a seat. They serve in order to become accepted, pray in order to make God favorably disposed, resist temptation in order to prove they are spiritual, and labor in ministry to secure identity. The result is exhaustion because the Christian life becomes a probationary examination.

Ephesians says the examination has already been passed by Another. The believer is “accepted in the beloved,” as older English translations put it, or graced in the Beloved. The Christian begins inside Christ's acceptance.

Blessed with Every Spiritual Blessing

Paul opens Ephesians with a cascade of praise: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who hath blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ” (Ephesians 1:3, ASV).

The grammar matters. God “hath blessed.” The blessings are located “in Christ.” The believer's fundamental spiritual wealth is not a future possibility waiting to be earned but a present inheritance in the Son.

Nee used this to challenge a poverty mentality in Christian spirituality. Believers often ask God to give what He has already given in Christ. They pray as though they were spiritual beggars standing outside the Father's house, when Ephesians describes them as adopted children with an inheritance.

This does not mean every blessing is presently experienced in fullness. Redemption has an already-and-not-yet structure. We await the redemption of the body and the consummation of all things. But the decisive gift has been given: Christ Himself.

Paul says God chose us in Christ, predestined us unto adoption, bestowed grace upon us in the Beloved, gave redemption through His blood, made known the mystery of His will, sealed us with the Holy Spirit, and provided the Spirit as earnest of our inheritance (Ephesians 1:4-14).

Each phrase directs attention away from self-produced spirituality. The Father plans, the Son accomplishes, the Spirit seals. Salvation is Trinitarian grace.

Nee's stress on position is healthiest when read inside this worshipful framework. “Sitting” is not a technique for avoiding responsibility. It is the posture of a person overwhelmed by divine initiative.

Chosen in Christ

“Even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blemish before him in love” (Ephesians 1:4, ASV).

Christians have disputed the relation between divine election and human response for centuries. Nee did not make this controversy the center of his ministry. He was more interested in the pastoral effect of Paul's words: the Christian's story begins in God's purpose, not in human accident.

This gives stability. A believer may look at his history and see a chain of failures, wounds, foolish decisions, and unlikely circumstances. Ephesians lifts his eyes farther back. Before the foundation of the world, God's redemptive purpose was already centered in Christ.

The purpose is not merely rescue from hell. Paul says “that we should be holy.” Grace has an intended moral shape. Election is not a reason for spiritual complacency but for worship and holiness.

Nee repeatedly warned against separating position from condition. To know we are seated in Christ is not to claim that every aspect of conduct is automatically mature. It is to locate the source from which transformation proceeds.

A child does not obey in order to become a child; he obeys because he is a child. Adoption precedes filial life.

Paul writes that God foreordained us “unto adoption as sons through Jesus Christ unto himself” (Ephesians 1:5, ASV). The Christian's obedience is therefore the response of belonging, not the audition of an orphan.

Redemption Through His Blood

“In whom we have our redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace” (Ephesians 1:7, ASV).

Nee never meant “sit” to detach the believer from the cross. The heavenly position exists only because Christ descended into death. Grace is free to us because it was costly to Him.

The phrase “riches of his grace” was important to Nee's vision. God does not forgive reluctantly, as though mercy were an exception reluctantly extracted from a severe Deity. Redemption displays the abundance of God's grace.

This is pastorally significant for believers whose consciences remain trapped in self-condemnation. A person can confess a sin repeatedly, not because repentance is incomplete but because he cannot accept that Christ's blood is sufficient. Repeated confession becomes an attempt to supplement the cross with emotional payment.

The answer is not to minimize sin. It is to maximize the value of Christ's sacrifice.

Hebrews says, “having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holy place by the blood of Jesus” (Hebrews 10:19, ASV). Boldness is not personality. It is access purchased by blood.

Nee's emphasis on the believer's position becomes precious here. We do not sit in heavenly places because we behaved our way upward. We sit because the crucified and risen Christ carried us in Himself.

The Eyes of the Heart

Paul's first great prayer in Ephesians is not that believers receive more possessions but that they see what is already theirs.

He asks God to give “a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him; having the eyes of your heart enlightened” (Ephesians 1:17-18, ASV).

Nee often used the language of “seeing.” To him, revelation was not primarily new information beyond the Bible but spiritual apprehension of biblical reality. A doctrine may be objectively true and yet function as though absent because the believer has not grasped its significance.

Paul wants the Ephesians to know the hope of God's calling, the riches of the glory of His inheritance in the saints, and “the exceeding greatness of his power to us-ward who believe” (Ephesians 1:19, ASV).

That power is measured by the resurrection of Christ.

The Christian's problem, then, is not merely lack of effort. It may be lack of sight. If we see ourselves primarily as isolated, under-resourced individuals trying to reach God, our spiritual life will reflect that premise. If we see ourselves as incorporated into the risen Christ, seated with Him, sealed by the Spirit, and brought near to the Father, our obedience begins from another place.

This is not positive thinking. The object is not a better image of the self but Christ.

Resurrection Power

Paul describes God's power as that “which he wrought in Christ, when he raised him from the dead, and made him to sit at his right hand in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 1:20, ASV).

Nee's spirituality is saturated with resurrection. He did not treat resurrection merely as proof that Jesus' atoning death was accepted. Resurrection is the beginning of a new creation and the power in which Christian life proceeds.

Death is the boundary natural strength cannot cross. Human skill can reorganize, rehabilitate, educate, discipline, and motivate. It cannot raise the dead. Resurrection is God's distinctive act.

This is why Nee could speak of circumstances of weakness as opportunities to know resurrection. If we possess sufficient natural energy for every task, we may never discover the difference between natural life and divine supply.

Paul wrote from his own extremity: “we had the sentence of death within ourselves, that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God who raiseth the dead” (2 Corinthians 1:9, ASV).

The purpose was not a romantic fascination with suffering. It was a transfer of trust.

Christian ministry often prays for resurrection power while carefully arranging life so that resurrection is unnecessary. We prefer capacities we can control. Nee challenges that instinct. God may allow us to reach the end of our resources so that the source becomes unmistakable.

Head Over All Things to the Church

Ephesians 1 moves from Christ's exaltation to the church: God “put all things in subjection under his feet, and gave him to be head over all things to the church, which is his body” (Ephesians 1:22-23, ASV).

Nee's teaching on “sit” therefore cannot be reduced to individual spirituality. We are seated with Christ as members of His Body. The church shares in the victory of its Head.

This shaped Nee's ecclesiology profoundly. Christ is not merely Head of individual Christians taken separately. He has a Body. The fullness of Christian life is corporate.

Western devotional reading often turns plural promises into private affirmations. Nee, writing in a culture with different communal assumptions and reading deeply in Pauline ecclesiology, repeatedly called believers back to the Body.

The individual believer may know Christ personally, but never privately in the sense of being detached from His people. “For in one Spirit were we all baptized into one body” (1 Corinthians 12:13, ASV).

This body dimension protects “sitting” from becoming spiritual self-absorption. We are not seated merely to feel secure. We are incorporated into God's purpose to display Christ through the church.

Dead, Made Alive, Raised, Seated

Ephesians 2 begins with an unflattering diagnosis: “And you did he make alive, when ye were dead through your trespasses and sins” (Ephesians 2:1, ASV).

The contrast could hardly be stronger. Dead people do not cooperate in resuscitating themselves. Paul wants grace to be seen as grace.

He describes humanity under the course of this world, the prince of the powers of the air, and the desires of the flesh. Then come two of Scripture's great words: “But God.”

“But God, being rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us ... made us alive together with Christ” (Ephesians 2:4-5, ASV).

Nee loved the sequence: made alive, raised, seated. All three are joined to Christ.

This is the spiritual logic behind resting. We cannot make ourselves alive, raise ourselves, or seat ourselves in heavenly places. God does it in Christ.

“For by grace have ye been saved through faith; and that not of yourselves, it is the gift of God; not of works, that no man should glory” (Ephesians 2:8-9, ASV).

The exclusion of boasting is decisive. Human beings can turn even spiritual disciplines into trophies. Grace removes the ground of superiority.

Yet verse 10 prevents passivity: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God afore prepared that we should walk in them” (Ephesians 2:10, ASV).

We sit before we walk, but we do walk. Grace creates a working people.

Rest and Works

The relation between rest and works is easily misunderstood. Nee did not teach that Christians should become inert. His own life was extraordinarily active. He preached, wrote, traveled, organized conferences, trained workers, published literature, engaged in business, endured controversy, and maintained demanding correspondence.

His concern was the inward source of works.

Hebrews speaks of entering God's rest while also saying, “Let us therefore give diligence to enter into that rest” (Hebrews 4:11, ASV). Diligence and rest coexist because the rest is not inactivity; it is ceasing from works as a basis of acceptance and participating in God's accomplished purpose.

Jesus offers the same paradox: “Come unto me ... and I will give you rest,” then immediately, “Take my yoke upon you” (Matthew 11:28-29, ASV). Rest leads into a yoke. The difference is the Master who shares it.

Nee wanted Christian service to carry this quality. There is a kind of activity that comes from anxiety: if I do not hold everything together, it will collapse. There is another kind that comes from trust: God is working, and I am invited to participate.

The outward schedule may be equally full. The inward posture is completely different.

Near by the Blood

Ephesians 2 also addresses the great ethnic and covenantal divide between Jew and Gentile. Gentiles once “were separate from Christ” and “strangers from the covenants of the promise” (Ephesians 2:12, ASV). “But now in Christ Jesus ye that once were far off are made nigh in the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13, ASV).

Nee's teaching on the church drew heavily from this new humanity. Christ “made both one, and brake down the middle wall of partition” (Ephesians 2:14, ASV).

The gospel does not merely reconcile individuals vertically to God. It creates horizontal reconciliation in a new people.

This truth challenged racial, national, class, and denominational pride. In Republican China, Christianity carried complicated associations with Western power. Nee wanted Chinese believers to receive the gospel without remaining ecclesiastically subordinate to Western institutions. Yet Ephesians also prevented national Christianity from becoming the final goal. Christ creates one new man.

“For through him we both have our access in one Spirit unto the Father” (Ephesians 2:18, ASV).

One Son, one Spirit, one Father—therefore one household.

The church is not an alliance among people who naturally belong together. It is a miracle of reconciliation among people whose deepest common identity is Christ.

A Dwelling Place of God

Paul changes metaphors: believers are fellow-citizens, household members, and stones in a temple “growing into a holy temple in the Lord” (Ephesians 2:21, ASV).

“In whom ye also are builded together for a habitation of God in the Spirit” (Ephesians 2:22, ASV).

Nee's church vision took “builded together” seriously. Christian maturity is not merely the perfection of individual stones. A polished stone lying by itself is not a temple.

This emphasis challenged intensely private spirituality. A believer may read the Bible deeply, pray long hours, and cultivate personal holiness while remaining unable to live with other Christians. Nee would question the maturity of such spirituality.

The church is the place where character is tested in relationship. Patience requires people who test patience. Forgiveness requires offenses. Humility appears when preferences collide. Love becomes concrete when someone is inconvenient.

Nee's later teaching on brokenness was therefore inseparable from church life. God uses fellow believers as instruments of formation.

This truth also needs boundaries. “Building together” must not be used to trap people in abusive environments or silence legitimate concerns. The same New Testament that commands unity also commands correction, discipline of leaders, protection of the vulnerable, and separation from persistent destructive behavior.

Biblical community is neither individualism nor coercive collectivism. It is life together under Christ.

The Mystery Hidden and Revealed

Ephesians 3 calls the church part of a “mystery” once hidden and now revealed: Gentiles are “fellow-heirs, and fellow-members of the body, and fellow-partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel” (Ephesians 3:6, ASV).

Nee's reading of God's eternal purpose gave the church immense significance. The church is not Plan B after Israel or merely a rescue shelter for sinners awaiting heaven. In Christ, God is displaying His wisdom through a people.

Paul says that “through the church the manifold wisdom of God” is made known “unto the principalities and the powers in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 3:10, ASV).

This cosmic language fascinated Nee. Church life has significance beyond what the visible congregation can measure. The unity, holiness, love, and testimony of believers participate in God's larger purpose.

Such a vision can inspire costly devotion. It can also tempt movements to overestimate their own special place in history. The church universal is larger than any network, including Nee's. The “manifold wisdom of God” is not the possession of one movement.

The safest application is worshipful humility: God is doing something through His whole people that exceeds our local importance.

Strengthened in the Inner Man

Paul's second prayer in Ephesians moves inward: “that he would grant you, according to the riches of his glory, that ye may be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inward man; that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith” (Ephesians 3:16-17, ASV).

Nee's vocabulary of the inner man later became more technical, but here the biblical emphasis is clear. The Spirit strengthens believers inwardly so that Christ's presence becomes experientially settled and formative.

The goal is not private mystical intensity. Paul prays that believers may be “rooted and grounded in love” and comprehend “with all the saints” the vast dimensions of Christ's love (Ephesians 3:17-18, ASV).

Again, the corporate phrase matters: “with all the saints.” No individual has enough perspective to grasp Christ's fullness alone.

Paul ends with abundance: God “is able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that worketh in us” (Ephesians 3:20, ASV).

Nee heard in this prayer the transition from position to experience. The believer is already in Christ, yet he needs strengthening to live from that reality. Objective grace becomes subjective formation by the Spirit.

Sitting Does Not Mean Spiritual Presumption

There is a false way to use positional truth. A Christian can quote that he is “seated in heavenly places” while neglecting repentance, wisdom, accountability, and ordinary responsibility. Spiritual language becomes a shield against reality.

Paul never allows this. The same letter that celebrates grace will soon command believers to tell the truth, work honestly, forgive one another, reject sexual immorality, honor marriage, raise children faithfully, and resist evil.

Position does not make practice irrelevant. It makes practice possible and properly motivated.

John warns, “He that saith he abideth in him ought himself also to walk even as he walked” (1 John 2:6, ASV).

The test of “sitting” is not how elevated our vocabulary becomes but whether grace produces the character of Christ.

Nee's own movement sometimes attracted readers who loved spiritual categories. His best teaching continually pushed them back toward reality. If revelation does not lead to obedience, it has not been rightly received.

The End of Spiritual Anxiety

At its pastoral best, “sit” is an answer to anxious Christianity.

Some believers live as though God were perpetually disappointed, His acceptance fluctuating minute by minute according to performance. Prayer becomes an attempt to regain favor. Bible reading becomes a quota. Service becomes proof of worth. Failure produces not healthy repentance but existential collapse.

Ephesians speaks a better word. In Christ we have redemption. In Christ we are chosen. In Christ we are made alive. In Christ we are raised. In Christ we are seated. In Christ we have access to the Father.

The repeated phrase is the foundation: in Christ.

Faith rests there.

Only then does Paul say, “I therefore ... beseech you to walk worthily of the calling wherewith ye were called” (Ephesians 4:1, ASV).

The “therefore” is the bridge. Chapters 1-3 have given the calling; chapters 4-6 describe the walk.

Nee's three-word summary now moves to its second word. The seated believer rises—not to earn grace, but because grace has given him a life worth walking.

“In Christ” as Paul's Spiritual Geography

Ephesians uses “in Christ,” “in him,” and related phrases repeatedly. Nee treated this language almost as spiritual geography. Just as a person located inside a room shares the room's environment, the believer located in Christ shares the consequences of Christ's history.

The analogy is limited, but it helps. If Noah's family is inside the ark, the ark's destiny becomes theirs. If humanity is in Adam, Adam's fall defines the old creation. If believers are in Christ, His death, resurrection, and acceptance define their new position.

Paul says, “if any man is in Christ, he is a new creature” (2 Corinthians 5:17, ASV).

The gospel is therefore not merely Christ doing something for people at a distance. It brings them into Himself.

Access to the Father

“Sitting” includes access. “In whom we have boldness and access in confidence through our faith in him” (Ephesians 3:12, ASV).

Many Christians live as though prayer requires climbing a spiritual mountain before God will listen. Ephesians says access is already opened in Christ.

This changes confession. We do not confess in order to persuade God to become Father again. We confess because the way to the Father remains open through Christ.

It changes worship. We do not create God's presence through music; we approach through the Son by the Spirit.

“For through him we both have our access in one Spirit unto the Father” (Ephesians 2:18, ASV).

Nee's teaching on position can therefore be deeply Trinitarian when read carefully.

Rest Before Crisis

A soldier should learn where he stands before battle begins. Nee's order has pastoral wisdom because crisis is a bad time to construct identity from scratch.

When accusation, illness, financial fear, or persecution comes, believers need truths already rooted: God has loved us; Christ has redeemed us; the Spirit has sealed us; we belong to the Body; resurrection is promised.

The time to learn to sit is before the earthquake.

Psalm 46 says, “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble” (Psalm 46:1, ASV). Refuge is not improvised by panic. It is entered.

Seated With Christ: Grace Before Performance

Nee's short exposition of Ephesians became famous because of a simple observation about order. Ephesians begins not with the believer walking or fighting, but with God seating Christ at His right hand and seating believers with Him. Only later does Paul command a worthy walk and describe spiritual conflict.

That order was not a literary curiosity for Nee. It expressed the logic of grace. Christian obedience grows from a position received before it becomes a path walked.

Paul writes that God “raised us up with him, and made us to sit with him in the heavenly places, in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 2:6, ASV). The verbs describe divine action. The believer does not climb into the heavenly places by spiritual achievement. God acts because of His mercy and because of union with Christ.

To sit is therefore to cease trying to establish what God has already given. This does not mean inactivity. In the ancient world, sitting at the right hand of a ruler could signify completed victory, privilege, and participation in authority. Christ is seated because His redemptive work is accomplished. The believer's rest is participation in that accomplished work.

Nee saw this as a cure for anxious religion. Many Christians begin each day as though they must persuade God to accept them. A failure creates distance; a successful devotional time creates confidence; praise inflates; criticism collapses. Identity rises and falls with performance. Ephesians begins elsewhere: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who hath blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ” (Ephesians 1:3, ASV).

The blessing is in Christ before it is in our feelings.

This emphasis is especially valuable for leaders. Ministry creates a relentless scoreboard: attendance, conversions, donations, growth, invitations, downloads, influence, buildings, staff, reputation. None of these measures is inherently wrong. Stewardship should be evaluated. But when metrics become identity, service becomes slavery. The seated believer can face a poor result honestly without treating it as a verdict on personal worth.

Ephesians also prevents rest from becoming individualistic. The same grace that seats believers with Christ creates “one new man” from divided peoples and builds them together into a dwelling place of God (Ephesians 2:15, 22, ASV). Rest in Christ is communal. The believer is not seated alone in a private spiritual suite.

This has ethical consequences. If grace places Jewish and Gentile believers together in Christ, then social superiority contradicts the position. Race, class, education, wealth, nationality, and religious pedigree cannot become grounds of boasting. Paul asks, in effect, what do you possess that you did not receive?

Nee's own movement sometimes struggled to embody this expansive unity, but his best teaching points toward it. To sit with Christ is to discover that every genuine believer is there by the same mercy. No one occupies a higher seat because of spiritual vocabulary.

The seated position also changes prayer. Ephesians 1 and 3 contain prayers not primarily for new possessions but for enlightened perception and strengthened apprehension. Paul asks that believers know the hope of God's calling, the riches of His inheritance, the greatness of His power, and the love of Christ. Much Christian prayer asks God to give what He has already given in Christ because we have not yet seen what we possess.

Nee's language of “seeing” grew from this pattern. Spiritual progress often occurs when a biblical fact moves from abstract truth to governing conviction. The fact was true before the moment of illumination. But once seen, it rearranges behavior.

The danger is turning “sitting” into another technique: try harder to rest, refuse all effort, or suppress anxiety until one feels victorious. That defeats the point. Rest is not a spiritual mood manufactured by concentration. It is faith's response to Christ's sufficiency.

The Christian begins where Christ finished. From that seat, the walk can begin.

If we possess sufficient natural energy for every task, we may never discover the difference between natural life and divine supply. Paul wrote from his own extremity: “we had the sentence of death within ourselves, that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God who raiseth the dead” (2 Corinthians 1:9, ASV). The purpose was not a romantic fascination with suffering. It was a transfer of trust. Christian ministry often prays for resurrection power while carefully arranging life so that resurrection is unnecessary. We prefer capacities we can control. Nee challenges that instinct. God may allow us to reach the end of our resources so that the source becomes unmistakable. Head Over All Things to the Church Ephesians 1 moves from Christ's exaltation to the church: God “put all things in subjection under his feet, and gave him to be head over all things to the church, which is his body” (Ephesians 1:22-23, ASV). Nee's teaching on “sit” therefore cannot be reduced to individual spirituality. We are seated with Christ as members of His Body. The church shares in the victory of its Head. This shaped Nee's ecclesiology profoundly. Christ is not merely Head of individual Christians taken separately. He has a Body. The fullness of Christian life is corporate. Western devotional reading often turns plural promises into private affirmations. Nee, writing in a culture with different communal assumptions and reading deeply in Pauline ecclesiology, repeatedly called believers back to the Body. The individual believer may know Christ personally, but never privately in the sense of being detached from His people. “For in one Spirit were we all baptized into one body” (1 Corinthians 12:13, ASV). This body dimension protects “sitting” from becoming spiritual self-absorption. We are not seated merely to feel secure. We are incorporated into God's purpose to display Christ through the church. Dead, Made Alive, Raised, Seated Ephesians 2 begins with an unflattering diagnosis: “And you did he make alive, when ye were dead through your trespasses and sins” (Ephesians 2:1, ASV). The contrast could hardly be stronger. Dead people do not cooperate in resuscitating themselves. Paul wants grace to be seen as grace. He describes humanity under the course of this world, the prince of the powers of the air, and the desires of the flesh. Then come two of Scripture's great words: “But God.” “But God, being rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us ... made us alive together with Christ” (Ephesians 2:4-5, ASV). Nee loved the sequence: made alive, raised, seated. All three are joined to Christ. This is the spiritual logic behind resting. We cannot make ourselves alive, raise ourselves, or seat ourselves in heavenly places. God does it in Christ. “For by grace have ye been saved through faith; and that not of yourselves, it is the gift of God; not of works, that no man should glory” (Ephesians 2:8-9, ASV). The exclusion of boasting is decisive. Human beings can turn even spiritual disciplines into trophies. Grace removes the ground of superiority. Yet verse 10 prevents passivity: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God afore prepared that we should walk in them” (Ephesians 2:10, ASV). We sit before we walk, but we do walk. Grace creates a working people. Rest and Works The relation between rest and works is easily misunderstood. Nee did not teach that Christians should become inert. His own life was extraordinarily active. He preached, wrote, traveled, organized conferences, trained workers, published literature, engaged in business, endured controversy, and maintained demanding correspondence. His concern was the inward source of works. Hebrews speaks of entering God's rest while also saying, “Let us therefore give diligence to enter into that rest” (Hebrews 4:11, ASV). Diligence and rest coexist because the rest is not inactivity; it is ceasing from works as a basis of acceptance and participating in God's accomplished purpose. Jesus offers the same paradox: “Come unto me ... and I will give you rest,” then immediately, “Take my yoke upon you” (Matthew 11:28-29, ASV). Rest leads into a yoke. The difference is the Master who shares it. Nee wanted Christian service to carry this quality. There is a kind of activity that comes from anxiety: if I do not hold everything together, it will collapse. There is another kind that comes from trust: God is working, and I am invited to participate. The outward schedule may be equally full. The inward posture is completely different. Near by the Blood Ephesians 2 also addresses the great ethnic and covenantal divide between Jew and Gentile. Gentiles once “were separate from Christ” and “strangers from the covenants of the promise” (Ephesians 2:12, ASV). “But now in Christ Jesus ye that once were far off are made nigh in the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13, ASV). Nee's teaching on the church drew heavily from this new humanity. Christ “made both one, and brake down the middle wall of partition” (Ephesians 2:14, ASV). The gospel does not merely reconcile individuals vertically to God. It creates horizontal reconciliation in a new people. This truth challenged racial, national, class, and denominational pride. In Republican China, Christianity carried complicated associations with Western power. Nee wanted Chinese believers to receive the gospel without remaining ecclesiastically subordinate to Western institutions. Yet Ephesians also prevented national Christianity from becoming the final goal. Christ creates one new man. “For through him we both have our access in one Spirit unto the Father” (Ephesians 2:18, ASV). One Son, one Spirit, one Father—therefore one household. The church is not an alliance among people who naturally belong together. It is a miracle of reconciliation among people whose deepest common identity is Christ. A Dwelling Place of God Paul changes metaphors: believers are fellow-citizens, household members, and stones in a temple “growing into a holy temple in the Lord” (Ephesians 2:21, ASV). “In whom ye also are builded together for a habitation of God in the Spirit” (Ephesians 2:22, ASV). Nee's church vision took “builded together” seriously. Christian maturity is not merely the perfection of individual stones. A polished stone lying by itself is not a temple. This emphasis challenged intensely private spirituality. A believer may read the Bible deeply, pray long hours, and cultivate personal holiness while remaining unable to live with other Christians. Nee would question the maturity of such spirituality. The church is the place where character is tested in relationship. Patience requires people who test patience. Forgiveness requires offenses. Humility appears when preferences collide. Love becomes concrete when someone is inconvenient. Nee's later teaching on brokenness was therefore inseparable from church life. God uses fellow believers as instruments of formation. This truth also needs boundaries. “Building together” must not be used to trap people in abusive environments or silence legitimate concerns. The same New Testament that commands unity also commands correction, discipline of leaders, protection of the vulnerable, and separation from persistent destructive behavior. Biblical community is neither individualism nor coercive collectivism. It is life together under Christ. The Mystery Hidden and Revealed Ephesians 3 calls the church part of a “mystery” once hidden and now revealed: Gentiles are “fellow-heirs, and fellow-members of the body, and fellow-partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel” (Ephesians 3:6, ASV). Nee's reading of God's eternal purpose gave the church immense significance. The church is not Plan B after Israel or merely a rescue shelter for sinners awaiting heaven. In Christ, God is displaying His wisdom through a people. Paul says that “through the church the manifold wisdom of God” is made known “unto the principalities and the powers in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 3:10, ASV). This cosmic language fascinated Nee. Church life has significance beyond what the visible congregation can measure. The unity, holiness, love, and testimony of believers participate in God's larger purpose. Such a vision can inspire costly devotion. It can also tempt movements to overestimate their own special place in history. The church universal is larger than any network, including Nee's. The “manifold wisdom of God” is not the possession of one movement. The safest application is worshipful humility: God is doing something through His whole people that exceeds our local importance. Strengthened in the Inner Man Paul's second prayer in Ephesians moves inward: “that he would grant you, according to the riches of his glory, that ye may be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inward man; that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith” (Ephesians 3:16-17, ASV). Nee's vocabulary of the inner man later became more technical, but here the biblical emphasis is clear. The Spirit strengthens believers inwardly so that Christ's presence becomes experientially settled and formative. The goal is not private mystical intensity. Paul prays that believers may be “rooted and grounded in love” and comprehend “with all the saints” the vast dimensions of Christ's love (Ephesians 3:17-18, ASV). Again, the corporate phrase matters: “with all the saints.” No individual has enough perspective to grasp Christ's fullness alone. Paul ends with abundance: God “is able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that worketh in us” (Ephesians 3:20, ASV). Nee heard in this prayer the transition from position to experience. The believer is already in Christ, yet he needs strengthening to live from that reality. Objective grace becomes subjective formation by the Spirit. Sitting Does Not Mean Spiritual Presumption There is a false way to use positional truth. A Christian can quote that he is “seated in heavenly places” while neglecting repentance, wisdom, accountability, and ordinary responsibility. Spiritual language becomes a shield against reality. Paul never allows this. The same letter that celebrates grace will soon command believers to tell the truth, work honestly, forgive one another, reject sexual immorality, honor marriage, raise children faithfully, and resist evil. Position does not make practice irrelevant. It makes practice possible and properly motivated. John warns, “He that saith he abideth in him ought himself also to walk even as he walked” (1 John 2:6, ASV). The test of “sitting” is not how elevated our vocabulary becomes but whether grace produces the character of Christ. Nee's own movement sometimes attracted readers who loved spiritual categories. His best teaching continually pushed them back toward reality. If revelation does not lead to obedience, it has not been rightly received. The End of Spiritual Anxiety At its pastoral best, “sit” is an answer to anxious Christianity. Some believers live as though God were perpetually disappointed, His acceptance fluctuating minute by minute according to performance. Prayer becomes an attempt to regain favor. Bible reading becomes a quota. Service becomes proof of worth. Failure produces not healthy repentance but existential collapse. Ephesians speaks a better word. In Christ we have redemption. In Christ we are chosen. In Christ we are made alive. In Christ we are raised. In Christ we are seated. In Christ we have access to the Father. The repeated phrase is the foundation: in Christ. Faith rests there. Only then does Paul say, “I therefore ... beseech you to walk worthily of the calling wherewith ye were called” (Ephesians 4:1, ASV). The “therefore” is the bridge. Chapters 1-3 have given the calling; chapters 4-6 describe the walk. Nee's three-word summary now moves to its second word. The seated believer rises—not to earn grace, but because grace has given him a life worth walking. “In Christ” as Paul's Spiritual Geography Ephesians uses “in Christ,” “in him,” and related phrases repeatedly. Nee treated this language almost as spiritual geography. Just as a person located inside a room shares the room's environment, the believer located in Christ shares the consequences of Christ's history. The analogy is limited, but it helps. If Noah's family is inside the ark, the ark's destiny becomes theirs. If humanity is in Adam, Adam's fall defines the old creation. If believers are in Christ, His death, resurrection, and acceptance define their new position. Paul says, “if any man is in Christ, he is a new creature” (2 Corinthians 5:17, ASV). The gospel is therefore not merely Christ doing something for people at a distance. It brings them into Himself. Access to the Father “Sitting” includes access. “In whom we have boldness and access in confidence through our faith in him” (Ephesians 3:12, ASV). Many Christians live as though prayer requires climbing a spiritual mountain before God will listen. Ephesians says access is already opened in Christ. This changes confession. We do not confess in order to persuade God to become Father again. We confess because the way to the Father remains open through Christ. It changes worship. We do not create God's presence through music; we approach through the Son by the Spirit. “For through him we both have our access in one Spirit unto the Father” (Ephesians 2:18, ASV). Nee's teaching on position can therefore be deeply Trinitarian when read carefully. Rest Before Crisis A soldier should learn where he stands before battle begins. Nee's order has pastoral wisdom because crisis is a bad time to construct identity from scratch. When accusation, illness, financial fear, or persecution comes, believers need truths already rooted: God has loved us; Christ has redeemed us; the Spirit has sealed us; we belong to the Body; resurrection is promised. The time to learn to sit is before the earthquake. Psalm 46 says, “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble” (Psalm 46:1, ASV). Refuge is not improvised by panic. It is entered. Seated With Christ: Grace Before Performance Nee's short exposition of Ephesians became famous because of a simple observation about order. Ephesians begins not with the believer walking or fighting, but with God seating Christ at His right hand and seating believers with Him. Only later does Paul command a worthy walk and describe spiritual conflict. That order was not a literary curiosity for Nee. It expressed the logic of grace. Christian obedience grows from a position received before it becomes a path walked. Paul writes that God “raised us up with him, and made us to sit with him in the heavenly places, in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 2:6, ASV). The verbs describe divine action. The believer does not climb into the heavenly places by spiritual achievement. God acts because of His mercy and because of union with Christ. To sit is therefore to cease trying to establish what God has already given. This does not mean inactivity. In the ancient world, sitting at the right hand of a ruler could signify completed victory, privilege, and participation in authority. Christ is seated because His redemptive work is accomplished. The believer's rest is participation in that accomplished work. Nee saw this as a cure for anxious religion. Many Christians begin each day as though they must persuade God to accept them. A failure creates distance; a successful devotional time creates confidence; praise inflates; criticism collapses. Identity rises and falls with performance. Ephesians begins elsewhere: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who hath blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ” (Ephesians 1:3, ASV). The blessing is in Christ before it is in our feelings. This emphasis is especially valuable for leaders. Ministry creates a relentless scoreboard: attendance, conversions, donations, growth, invitations, downloads, influence, buildings, staff, reputation. None of these measures is inherently wrong. Stewardship should be evaluated. But when metrics become identity, service becomes slavery. The seated believer can face a poor result honestly without treating it as a verdict on personal worth. Ephesians also prevents rest from becoming individualistic. The same grace that seats believers with Christ creates “one new man” from divided peoples and builds them together into a dwelling place of God (Ephesians 2:15, 22, ASV). Rest in Christ is communal. The believer is not seated alone in a private spiritual suite. This has ethical consequences. If grace places Jewish and Gentile believers together in Christ, then social superiority contradicts the position. Race, class, education, wealth, nationality, and religious pedigree cannot become grounds of boasting. Paul asks, in effect, what do you possess that you did not receive? Nee's own movement sometimes struggled to embody this expansive unity, but his best teaching points toward it. To sit with Christ is to discover that every genuine believer is there by the same mercy. No one occupies a higher seat because of spiritual vocabulary. The seated position also changes prayer. Ephesians 1 and 3 contain prayers not primarily for new possessions but for enlightened perception and strengthened apprehension. Paul asks that believers know the hope of God's calling, the riches of His inheritance, the greatness of His power, and the love of Christ. Much Christian prayer asks God to give what He has already given in Christ because we have not yet seen what we possess. Nee's language of “seeing” grew from this pattern. Spiritual progress often occurs when a biblical fact moves from abstract truth to governing conviction. The fact was true before the moment of illumination. But once seen, it rearranges behavior. The danger is turning “sitting” into another technique: try harder to rest, refuse all effort, or suppress anxiety until one feels victorious. That defeats the point. Rest is not a spiritual mood manufactured by concentration. It is faith's response to Christ's sufficiency. The Christian begins where Christ finished. From that seat, the walk can begin.

fields.title: Walk: Christ Lived Through Us
fields.body_html:
The Therefore of Ephesians

After three chapters of announcing what God has done, Paul turns to the believer's conduct: “I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beseech you to walk worthily of the calling wherewith ye were called” (Ephesians 4:1, ASV).

Watchman Nee built the second movement of Sit, Walk, Stand around this word: walk. The Christian who has learned to rest in Christ does not remain motionless. Grace creates a manner of life.

The “therefore” is vital. Christian ethics are not free-floating rules imposed upon strangers. They are the family likeness expected of those who have been brought into God's household. Paul does not say, Walk worthily so that you may be called. He says, Walk worthily of the calling already received.

Nee saw this as the cure for both legalism and carelessness. Legalism disconnects obedience from grace and makes conduct a ladder toward acceptance. Carelessness disconnects grace from obedience and treats acceptance as permission to remain unchanged. Ephesians refuses both.

“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works” (Ephesians 2:10, ASV). Works do not create the new creation; the new creation produces works.

The Christian walk therefore becomes the visible expression of an invisible position.

Lowliness, Meekness, Longsuffering

Paul's first description of a worthy walk is not brilliance, courage, doctrinal sophistication, or supernatural power. It is “with all lowliness and meekness, with longsuffering, forbearing one another in love” (Ephesians 4:2, ASV).

Nee's spirituality is sometimes remembered for high concepts—resurrection life, spiritual authority, the overcomer, heavenly position. But the New Testament tests all elevated language by ordinary humility.

Lowliness refuses the need to be superior. Meekness is strength under God's government. Longsuffering gives people time. Forbearance makes room for the unfinished work of grace in others.

These qualities are essential because the church consists of redeemed sinners being transformed. Any ecclesiology that requires everyone to be easy to live with before unity is possible will never produce a church.

Paul says believers should give “diligence to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4:3, ASV). They do not create the unity; the Spirit has created one Body. Their task is to keep it.

Nee's anti-denominational vision drew heavily from this fact. Yet Ephesians places the maintenance of unity in the context of humility, patience, and love. Correct ecclesiology without these virtues contradicts itself.

A person may argue passionately for one Body while treating fellow Christians contemptuously. In doing so he denies with conduct the doctrine he defends with words.

One Body, One Spirit, One Lord

“There is one body, and one Spirit ... one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all” (Ephesians 4:4-6, ASV).

Nee regarded this unity as objective. Christians do not become one by joining the same organization; they are one because they share the same Christ and Spirit.

This truth has radical implications. A believer from another denomination who truly belongs to Christ is spiritually nearer to us than an unbeliever who shares our nationality, politics, education, or culture. Christ creates a deeper kinship.

Nee wanted church practice to acknowledge that fact. He resisted names that divided believers according to founders or secondary doctrines. His vision resonates with Jesus' prayer “that they may all be one” (John 17:21, ASV).

But unity is not the same as doctrinal indifference. The New Testament also commands the church to guard the gospel, reject false teaching about Christ, and exercise discipline. “One faith” has content.

The challenge is to distinguish essentials that define Christian fellowship from secondary convictions around which believers may differ. Nee sometimes drew that line differently from other Christians, especially regarding baptism, local church ground, and communion. His own movement's history shows how difficult the task is.

The enduring principle is that fellowship should begin with what God has done in making believers one, not with our capacity to construct an institution large enough to contain them.

Gifts Are Given for the Body

Paul moves from unity to diversity: “But unto each one of us was the grace given according to the measure of the gift of Christ” (Ephesians 4:7, ASV).

One Body does not mean uniformity. Christ distributes gifts.

Nee strongly emphasized the functioning of every member. Leaders do not constitute the Body while ordinary Christians attend. Every member has a place in the life and service of the church.

Ephesians lists apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers, given “for the perfecting of the saints, unto the work of ministering, unto the building up of the body of Christ” (Ephesians 4:12, ASV).

The punctuation and interpretation of this verse have been discussed, but the broad movement is clear: gifted leaders equip the saints, and the Body is built as members function.

Nee's assemblies attempted to embody this through participatory meetings and lay ministry. The principle remains relevant even in churches with more structured services. The question is whether believers are being equipped to minister outside the platform.

A church can have excellent sermons and still be immature if members never learn to pray with the suffering, explain the gospel, disciple younger believers, reconcile conflict, use spiritual gifts, and serve neighbors.

The goal is “a fullgrown man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ” (Ephesians 4:13, ASV). Spiritual maturity is measured by Christ's likeness, not by institutional sophistication.

No Longer Children

Paul wants believers to be “no longer children, tossed to and fro and carried about with every wind of doctrine” (Ephesians 4:14, ASV).

Nee lived in a Christian world crowded with movements, prophetic schemes, holiness teachings, missionary appeals, denominational claims, and new religious groups. He read broadly and was himself a strong theological innovator. He therefore knew both the value and danger of spiritual novelty.

Immaturity is easily impressed. It mistakes intensity for truth, novelty for revelation, confidence for authority, and unusual vocabulary for depth.

Paul's answer is not cynicism but maturity through truth and love: “speaking truth in love, may grow up in all things into him, who is the head, even Christ” (Ephesians 4:15, ASV).

Truth without love can become a weapon. Love without truth becomes sentimentality. Growth requires both.

This verse also provides a safeguard for reading Nee. His teachings should be tested, not merely admired. The right response to a gifted teacher is not uncritical loyalty but grateful discernment under Scripture.

Nee himself urged believers to know the Word. No later disciple honors him by treating his books as a second canon.

The Supply of Every Joint

Ephesians pictures the Body “fitly framed and knit together through that which every joint supplieth, according to the working in due measure of each several part” (Ephesians 4:16, ASV).

Nee loved the word supply. Christian relationships are not merely administrative connections. Members receive Christ and minister Christ to one another.

The metaphor implies dependence. A hand detached from the body cannot remain healthy by insisting on its individual rights. Neither can the body ignore the hand.

Nee sometimes spoke of “Body consciousness”—an awareness that one's life and ministry belong within a larger organism. This challenged the independent Christian worker who builds a private kingdom.

Paul's own ministry reflects interdependence. He needed Barnabas, Silas, Timothy, Luke, Priscilla and Aquila, churches that prayed and gave, and even unnamed believers who refreshed him. Apostolic authority did not eliminate need.

For leaders, this is humbling. The more visible a ministry becomes, the easier it is to imagine that others are extensions of the leader's calling. Ephesians reverses the image: the leader is one member supplying what Christ gives, while receiving the supply of others.

The Body grows “unto the building up of itself in love” (Ephesians 4:16, ASV). Love is not decorative. It is the atmosphere of organic growth.

Put Off and Put On

Paul now becomes intensely practical. Believers should no longer walk “as the Gentiles also walk, in the vanity of their mind” (Ephesians 4:17, ASV). They have “learned Christ” differently.

The phrase is striking. Christianity is not merely learning Christian rules; it is learning Christ.

Paul describes putting away the old man and putting on the new, “which after God hath been created in righteousness and holiness of truth” (Ephesians 4:24, ASV).

Nee's Romans 6 teaching appears again. The old man has been crucified with Christ; therefore the believer puts off conduct belonging to the old life and puts on conduct consistent with the new.

This includes truthfulness: “Wherefore, putting away falsehood, speak ye truth each one with his neighbor” (Ephesians 4:25, ASV).

It includes anger disciplined before it becomes a foothold: “Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath” (Ephesians 4:26, ASV).

It includes honest labor and generosity: “Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labor ... that he may have whereof to give to him that hath need” (Ephesians 4:28, ASV).

The transformation is remarkable. The thief does not merely stop stealing; his hands become instruments of generosity. Grace redirects capacity.

The Tongue as an Instrument of Grace

“Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but such as is good for edifying as the need may be, that it may give grace to them that hear” (Ephesians 4:29, ASV).

Nee's teaching on spiritual ministry makes this verse especially searching. If Christian service is the release of Christ's life, words should carry grace.

This does not mean speech must always be gentle in tone. Jesus could rebuke hypocrisy sharply; Paul could confront error. But even correction should aim at edification rather than self-display.

The tongue reveals source. Gossip may feel like fellowship but tears down. Sarcasm can disguise contempt as humor. Flattery manipulates. Exaggeration serves image. Harsh truth can satisfy anger rather than restore a brother.

James says, “If any stumbleth not in word, the same is a perfect man, able to bridle the whole body also” (James 3:2, ASV).

The spiritual person is tested in speech.

Nee's own forceful style influenced generations of readers. The danger for disciples is to imitate certainty without sharing his years of formation. Spiritual authority is not created by speaking categorically.

The mature tongue is governed by truth, love, timing, and the needs of the hearer.

Grieving the Holy Spirit

“And grieve not the Holy Spirit of God, in whom ye were sealed unto the day of redemption” (Ephesians 4:30, ASV).

This verse joins assurance and responsibility. The Spirit seals the believer unto redemption; yet the believer can grieve Him.

Nee's devotional teaching placed great importance on sensitivity to the Spirit. He believed persistent disobedience could dull spiritual perception.

The context is relational sin: bitterness, wrath, anger, clamor, railing, malice. We sometimes imagine grieving the Spirit primarily through neglect of mystical exercises. Paul places the warning among ordinary human relationships.

“Be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving each other, even as God also in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32, ASV).

The Spirit's life looks like forgiveness.

The standard is the gospel: “even as God ... forgave you.” Christian forgiveness is not pretending an offense did not occur, nor does it always eliminate consequences or restore trust instantly. It means releasing vengeance and moving toward the mercy we ourselves have received.

For Nee, church life was one of God's principal classrooms for such transformation. Abstract spirituality is easy until another person wounds us.

Walk in Love

“Be ye therefore imitators of God, as beloved children; and walk in love, even as Christ also loved you, and gave himself up for us” (Ephesians 5:1-2, ASV).

The phrase “beloved children” again grounds the command in identity. We imitate because we are loved.

The definition of love is Christ's self-giving. Love is not mere affection; it takes the shape of the cross.

Nee's teaching on brokenness belongs here. The outer man is broken not to make a person gloomy or passive but to free him from self-centeredness so that the life of Christ can reach others. Genuine brokenness increases love.

Paul immediately contrasts love with sexual immorality, uncleanness, covetousness, filthiness, foolish talking, and coarse jesting (Ephesians 5:3-4). Love has moral boundaries. It does not baptize appetite.

This is important in an age that often defines love as affirmation of desire. New Testament love seeks the good of the other under God's truth.

Christ “gave himself up for us.” The cross remains the pattern.

Walk as Children of Light

“For ye were once darkness, but are now light in the Lord: walk as children of light” (Ephesians 5:8, ASV).

Paul does not merely say believers were in darkness; he says they were darkness. Nor does he merely say they possess light; they are light “in the Lord.” Identity again produces conduct.

“The fruit of the light is in all goodness and righteousness and truth” (Ephesians 5:9, ASV).

Nee's insistence on inward spiritual life can be tested here. Whatever “inner life” means, its fruit should be observable as goodness, righteousness, and truth. A person who claims unusual communion with God while living deceitfully has failed a biblical test.

“Have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather even reprove them” (Ephesians 5:11, ASV). Christian love does not require moral silence.

Yet exposure must begin with ourselves. It is easy for churches to denounce the darkness outside while hiding sin within. Walking in light includes confession and accountability.

John says, “If we say that we have fellowship with him and walk in the darkness, we lie” (1 John 1:6, ASV).

Spirituality and honesty are inseparable.

Walk Carefully

“Look therefore carefully how ye walk, not as unwise, but as wise; redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Ephesians 5:15-16, ASV).

Nee lived through extraordinary instability: warlord politics, nationalist revolution, Japanese invasion, civil war, Communist victory, ideological campaigns, imprisonment. “The days are evil” was not theoretical.

Wisdom meant understanding the Lord's will in changing circumstances. It required alertness rather than fear.

Paul continues, “be filled with the Spirit” (Ephesians 5:18, ASV). The filling of the Spirit produces worship, thanksgiving, and mutual submission.

Nee emphasized spiritual fullness, but Paul's signs are strikingly communal and ordinary: speaking in psalms, hymns and spiritual songs; giving thanks; subjecting yourselves one to another in the fear of Christ (Ephesians 5:19-21).

Spirit-filled life is not proved merely by unusual experiences. It is seen in worship, gratitude, and relationships ordered under Christ.

Marriage and the Mystery of Christ

Ephesians applies the Christian walk to marriage. The passage has generated intense debate, especially around submission and headship. Nee, shaped by his own cultural and theological setting, generally read the text in traditional terms. A responsible contemporary reading must keep the whole passage centered on Christ's self-giving.

“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself up for it” (Ephesians 5:25, ASV).

Whatever authority one believes the husband possesses, its model is a crucified Bridegroom. Christ does not exploit the church for His comfort. He gives Himself for her holiness and good.

The passage begins with “subjecting yourselves one to another in the fear of Christ” (Ephesians 5:21, ASV). Christian marriage cannot be reduced to privilege on one side and duty on the other. Both belong to Christ.

Nee's later emphasis on delegated authority must always be subordinated to this model. Authority that protects itself at another's expense has ceased to look like Jesus.

Marriage is ultimately a sign: “This mystery is great: but I speak in regard of Christ and of the church” (Ephesians 5:32, ASV).

The earthly relationship points beyond itself.

Children, Parents, Workers, Masters

Paul continues into household relationships. Children obey parents “in the Lord” (Ephesians 6:1, ASV), while fathers are warned, “provoke not your children to wrath: but nurture them in the chastening and admonition of the Lord” (Ephesians 6:4, ASV).

Authority is again bounded by responsibility.

Paul also addresses bondservants and masters within the first-century social order. These texts have tragically been misused to justify slavery. The New Testament does not offer a modern abolitionist treatise, but it plants principles that undermine human ownership: masters and servants share one Master in heaven, and “there is no respect of persons with him” (Ephesians 6:9, ASV).

The application to modern work should not erase the historical difference between employment and slavery. Yet Paul's insistence that work be done “as unto Christ” gives dignity to hidden labor.

Nee valued ordinary faithfulness. Spiritual life is not confined to meetings. The worker at a desk, parent in a kitchen, merchant negotiating honestly, student studying, and servant performing unnoticed tasks all have an arena for walking with Christ.

The test of spiritual teaching is Monday morning.

Christ Lived Through Us

What does “walk” finally mean for Nee? It does not mean copying Jesus externally as though He were merely an example standing outside us. It means allowing the indwelling Christ to express His life through yielded members.

Paul says, “It is no longer I that live, but Christ liveth in me” (Galatians 2:20, ASV).

Nee's language can sound as though the human personality disappears. Biblically, Paul remains an active “I”: “the life which I now live in the flesh I live in faith.” Union does not annihilate personhood; it reorders it around Christ.

The mature Christian does not become less human but more truly human in conformity to the image of the Son. Christ's life does not erase temperament, culture, memory, creativity, or calling. It sanctifies them.

To “let Christ live” is therefore not passivity. It is faith-filled obedience in continual dependence.

Failure on the Road

No Christian walks perfectly. The danger of a “victorious life” message is that failure can become difficult to admit. Believers may fear that confession proves they have not understood the secret.

The New Testament provides a better realism. “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1 John 1:8, ASV). Yet immediately: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9, ASV).

Grace not only begins the walk; grace restores us when we stumble.

Nee's best theology supports this. The blood of Christ remains the ground of fellowship. The cross remains God's answer to self. The Spirit remains our source. We never move beyond the gospel into a superior class of Christian existence where repentance is unnecessary.

A worthy walk includes quick confession.

Love as the Final Measure

Paul's picture of maturity culminates again and again in love. This is consistent with the whole New Testament.

“If I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:2, ASV).

A Christian may understand Nee's distinctions between spirit and soul, hold strong convictions about the local church, know Romans 6, speak of resurrection life, practice faith principles, and still miss the central moral evidence of Christ's life.

“The fruit of the Spirit is love” (Galatians 5:22, ASV). Love stands first.

Love is patient in meetings, honest in business, faithful in marriage, generous toward need, truthful in conflict, hospitable across differences, courageous toward sin, and forgiving after injury.

This is walking.

The seated believer walks through the ordinary world carrying the character of the One in whom he is seated.

But Ephesians has one more verb. The Christian does not only receive and walk. He inhabits a contested world. Evil resists the purposes of God. The church therefore must learn not merely to advance but, at decisive moments, to refuse retreat.

The final word is stand.

The Walk Is Relational Before It Is Spectacular

Christians are often attracted to extraordinary spirituality: miracles, visions, prophetic insight, heroic mission, intense prayer. Ephesians 4-6 spends much of its moral energy on relationships.

Tell the truth. Work honestly. Speak words that build. Forgive. Love your spouse. Raise children without provoking them. Do ordinary work as unto Christ.

This is important for reading Nee. His language can sound elevated, but the test of “Christ as life” is mundane.

“If a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar” (1 John 4:20, ASV).

The highest spirituality must survive the dining table.

Walking by the Spirit

Galatians provides a parallel to Ephesians: “Walk by the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh” (Galatians 5:16, ASV).

The fruit that follows is moral and relational: love, joy, peace, longsuffering, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, meekness, self-control.

Nee's language of spirit becomes safest when anchored here. The evidence of walking by the Spirit is not unusual inward sensation but Christlike fruit.

A person who claims spiritual intuition while lacking self-control has reason to question the claim.

Walking Worthily in Public Life

Nee often tried to keep the church separate from partisan politics, but Ephesians' call to a worthy walk still applies to public life. Christians pay taxes, conduct business, hold citizenship, encounter injustice, and influence communities.

“Walk in wisdom toward them that are without” (Colossians 4:5, ASV).

The church's public witness depends not only on what it says about Christ but how believers behave when no explicitly religious activity is occurring.

Business honesty, treatment of employees, speech about opponents, sexual integrity, and care for the poor all belong to the walk.
